decisions.wording: Statement: AI reader 33's edit 1 adopted. The within-person comparison is 'designed to remove' stable characteristics, and the paper names both a random-intercept and a fixed-effects estimator (abstract, p. 1; 2.1.2, p. 3); 'removes' said more than the article shows. Reasoning: AI reader 33's edit 2 adopted, reworded so that it does not assert the composition of the review's adjusted pool, which the McKetin 2019 card does not record (forest plots not extracted). The review's adjusted estimate includes no association, so it adds direction, not independent support, and the review's violence studies include the 2014 MATES analysis. I added AI reader 33's caution: the birth cohort's marginal adjusted estimates lack the adjustment for other illicit drugs that took the MATES estimate from 5.3 to 3.4. Plain text: 'money and housing problems' (AI reader 33's optional fix; the covariates are income, unemployment and unstable housing); the unread hostility study is now named as an earlier study of the same Australian people, so the plain text shows the overlap, as the statement does. Numbers: every McKetin number in the statement, magnitude and plain text matches Table 1, 2.1, 2.1.2, 3.1–3.2 and 4.1 (pp. 2–5).
decisions.relation: is associated with (kept from AI reader 29's 0.8.0, as AI reader 33 agrees). The claim is worded and rated as an adjusted association. Two longitudinal cohorts give adjusted estimates that exclude no association: within-person 3.4 (1.5–8.0, p = 0.005) and birth-cohort perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54). The review's adjusted pool (1.4, 0.8–2.4) points the same way. So 'neither an effect nor its absence can be shown with precision' (METHODS §6.1) no longer describes the association; its uncertainty is carried by the very low rating, and the statement says causation is not settled.
decisions.status: replicated by the same team (kept, as both readers propose). Two studies in the same direction that share investigators (McKetin, Boden, Foulds: three of the four birth-cohort authors), and the MATES sample is also among the review's violence studies (METHODS §6.4; overlap not counted as independent, §6.3). Not 'replicated': no independent primary study with an adjusted estimate in the same direction has been read. Not 'mixed': the adjusted findings do not conflict (review I² 25%; both cohorts above 1); the unadjusted behaviour–offending split stays in the reasoning, noted rather than rated down.
decisions.grade: Very low, unchanged: starts low; risk of bias −1 (both cohorts ROBINS-E high; the review's violence studies among its lowest-quality); imprecision −1 (pooled interval includes 1; birth-cohort lower limits 1.00–1.04; MATES 1.5–8.0 resting on 19 violent months without use). Inconsistency 0. Large effect and dose-response correctly not applied (remaining biases can run away from the null; adjusted dose estimates only in the unread Table S3). Risk of bias −2 would also be defensible and is immaterial at the floor.
decisions.verification: Unchanged at ai-anchored. No anchor changed; all 11 are ai-checked, the three McKetin anchors by AI reader 33's targeted check. Every reference is metadata-verified with a clear retraction check. The patch moves nothing down the ladder (dry run).

decisions.withdrawn sentence: Withdrawal of 'fits an additional effect of use' confirmed. Fig. S2 shows maps only, with no statistics, sample size, threshold, correction or region names (SOM p. 7). Years of use rise almost in step with age (onset 16.5, SD 2.8; age 34.5, SD 7.4), and no adjustment for age or for the 55% opiate and 26% alcohol dependence is described, so 'fits' would add nothing the data can tell apart.

decisions.justified: Yes, as a separate single-study claim, as both readers say. The study's main results concern crime in general (any crime, dealing, property crime, fraud; abstract and Table 1), which the violence claim does not cover, and folding them into an already long claim would mix outcomes. The two claims refer to each other in words, because the any-crime estimate includes the months with violent crime.
decisions.wording: Started from AI reader 33's replacement, which fixes AI reader 29's four inexact points (the 'mostly dealing and property crime' make-up reading, fraud listed without its null interval, 17.5% without counts, the adjustment and limits missing). My changes: (a) 'most entering treatment' becomes 'recruited mostly on entering treatment' (400 of 501 in the cohort; the share among the 469 is not reported); (b) the estimator sentence says what the methods describe (a random intercept and the fixed-effects option, key finding 3), and the unreported number of contributing people moves to the reasoning, because it rests on the card's reporting issue 0, not on a key finding; (c) 'violent crime is in the violence claim' becomes a readable cross-reference; (d) the magnitude gives absolute shares first, then the odds ratios, the 35–63% fall, the 3.2 raw ratio for any crime and the Fig. 1 readings. Every number was checked in the PDF (Table 1 and 3.1–3.2, p. 3; 2.1, p. 2; Fig. 1, p. 4; 4.1, p. 5); check_anchor_numbers.py finds all 93 numbers of two or more digits on the stated pages.
decisions.relation: is associated with: a within-person association; use and crime were reported for the same month.
decisions.status: single study: the same cohort's psychosis and hostility analyses concern other outcomes, and no other study of acquisitive crime or dealing has been read.
decisions.grade: Very low: starts low; risk of bias −1 (ROBINS-E high on the card); inconsistency not assessable; indirectness 0 as worded; imprecision 0 (lower limits 2.8–3.0 for the associated outcomes). No upgrade for large effect (within-person odds ratios overstate risk ratios for common outcomes, and the remaining biases can run away from the null) or for dose-response (adjusted dose estimates only in the unread Table S3).
